- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text: All ~5,150 probes agree with the spec's algorithm. I found one factual error in the spec's *explanation* of the abort (not the algorithm), plus one missing harness-level edge case.

apis.name: truncate(word, 5)
apis.pseudocode:
truncate(s: &[u8], len: usize = 5, omission: &[u8] = b"...") -> Vec<u8>

  // Pure BYTE operation. No UTF-8 awareness, no word/whitespace boundary logic,
  // no trimming, no case folding. Never observed to throw.

  1. if s.len() <= len:            // inclusive threshold: 5 bytes passes through, 6 truncates
         return s.to_vec()         // exact copy, including leading/trailing spaces, tabs,
                                   // control bytes (0x01..0x1F, 0x7F) and high bytes (0x80..0xFF)
  2. keep = len - omission.len()   // = 5 - 3 = 2 for the only call ever made
  3. return s[0 .. keep] ++ omission   // ALWAYS exactly 5 bytes: s[0], s[1], 0x2E, 0x2E, 0x2E

  Fully confirmed consequences:
   - For every s with s.len() >= 6 the output is byte-identical to s[0..2] ++ b"...",
     independent of s.len() (verified at every length 1..30, and at 100 / 1000 / 10000 /
     100000 / 60001 bytes).
   - s[0] and s[1] are RAW BYTES, copied verbatim. Exhaustively verified: for all 254 byte
     values X in 0x01..0xFF (excluding 0x0A, handled separately) the 6-byte words
     X."bcdef", "a".X."cdef" and "abcde".X produce X+'b'+"...", 'a'+X+"..." and "ab..."
     respectively -- no byte is special-cased, escaped, case-folded or validated.
   - It WILL cut a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence in half, emitting a lone lead byte (0xC3, 0xF0)
     or a lone continuation byte, with no replacement character and no error.
   - Whitespace is data: b"      " -> b"  ..."; b"    xy" -> b"  ..."; b"hello world" -> b"he...";
     b"a bcdefgh" -> b"a ..." (0x61 0x20 2E 2E 2E) -- the kept prefix is NOT right-trimmed.
   - 0x0A is an ordinary data byte too (it just breaks line-oriented harnesses, see edge cases).

evidence.output: 1..5 -> input verbatim; 6..30 -> 'zz...' (od: z z . . . \n) every time. Threshold confirmed <= 5.
od: 61 62 63 64 65 0a -- verbatim
od: 61 62 2e 2e 2e 0a
'QQ...' (od: 51 51 2e 2e 2e 0a) for all four -- no length-dependent behavior, no throw at 100 KB
line 17 = 'aa...'; the process completes normally, so truncate has no size limit

edge_cases: Threshold is INCLUSIVE: s.len() <= 5 returns the input verbatim; s.len() >= 6 always returns exactly 5 bytes. Verified at every length 1..30 and at 100/1000/10000/100000/60001.
Length is std::string::size(), i.e. BYTES, not characters. A 3-character/6-byte UTF-8 string IS truncated; a 3-character/5-byte one is NOT.
Only s[0] and s[1] survive. Exhaustively proven by three 254-value byte sweeps (byte 0, byte 1, last byte): no byte value is special-cased, so a Rust port needs zero classification logic here.

The prefix slice can split a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence, producing invalid UTF-8 (e.g. 61 C3 2E 2E 2E, F0 9F 2E 2E 2E). A faithful port must operate on Vec<u8>; `&s[..2]` on a &str would panic exactly where the C++ succeeds, and from_utf8_lossy would inject U+FFFD the C++ never emits.

No whitespace trimming (left or right), no word/separator boundary snapping, no Unicode ellipsis: the omission is three ASCII 0x2E bytes. 'a bcdefgh' -> 0x61 0x20 '...' is the decisive counter-example to any rstrip.
Bytes >= 0x80, control bytes 0x01..0x1F, 0x7F and 0x3A are all ordinary data.
Never throws or truncates early for any observed input, including 100 KB inputs.
Line 17's value is UNOBSERVABLE for the empty word and for any word ending in 0x3A, because line 18 kills the process before anything is printed (see demodulize).

apis.name: demodulize("Test::" + word)
apis.pseudocode:
demodulize(s: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8>   // may throw std::out_of_range

  // SURVIVING HYPOTHESIS (A):  pos = s.find_last_of(':');  return s.substr(pos + 2)
  // Falsified alternatives (all re-checked here):
  //   (B) pos = s.rfind("::"); substr(pos+3)   -- FALSIFIED by single-colon words
  //   (F) pos = s.find("::");  substr(pos+3)   -- FALSIFIED by the same words
  //   (E) pos = s.find(':');   substr(pos+2)   -- FALSIFIED by 'cat' -> "at" (E predicts "cat")
  // The bug in the original: it locates the last ':' BYTE but then advances by the length of
  // the "::" SEPARATOR, so it always eats one byte too many.

  1. pos = index of the LAST byte in s equal to 0x3A (':'); npos if none
  2. if pos == npos:  return s.to_vec()        // <-- UNREACHABLE via line 18, see uncertainties
  3. start = pos + 2
  4. if start > s.len():  throw std::out_of_range(
         "basic_string::substr: __pos (which is {start}) > this->size() (which is {s.len()})")
     // start == s.len() is LEGAL and yields the empty string
  5. return s[start ..].to_vec()

  ---- Specialised to line 18, where s = "Test::" ++ word, so s.len() == 6 + word.len() ----
  The literal prefix always supplies ':' at s[4] and s[5], so pos >= 5 and the npos branch
  never fires. Let m = word.len().

  * m == 0                        -> pos=5, start=7 > 6                      => ABORT (7, 6)
  * word contains no ':' (m >= 1) -> pos=5, start=7 <= 6+m                   => word[1..]
                                     (the word with its FIRST BYTE dropped: 'cat' -> 'at')
  * word's last ':' is at index j:
      pos = 6 + j, start = 8 + j
      - if j == m-1 (word ENDS with ':') -> start = m+7 > m+6                => ABORT (m+7, m+6)
      - else                             -> word[j+2 ..]
                                            (empty exactly when j == m-2)

  ==> ABORT (SIGABRT, exit 134, ZERO bytes on stdout) IFF word.is_empty() OR word's last
      byte is 0x3A. Otherwise the line is word[k..] with k = (last ':' index) + 2, else 1.

  All slicing is BYTE slicing; it routinely emits bare UTF-8 continuation bytes.

edge_cases: ABORT CONDITION (exact): line 18 throws std::out_of_range iff word.is_empty() OR word's last byte is 0x3A (':'). Independently established three ways: the 255-value single-byte scan (only 0x3A), the 253-value 'a'.X scan (only 0x3A), and the 253-value X.'bcde:' scan (all abort). Plus ~2600 randomized/exhaustive words with 0 mismatches.

CORRECTED MECHANISM: on abort the process emits ZERO bytes on stdout -- and this is NOT a buffering artifact. Verified with `stdbuf -o0`, under a pty (where stdout would be line-buffered), and with a word whose successful output is 1020035 bytes. The binary therefore computes all 20 result strings before writing any. A Rust port must collect all 20 lines and print only on success; printing incrementally would produce output the C++ never emits.

Exit status on abort is 134 (128 + SIGABRT), with a core dump; the stderr text is exactly: "terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::out_of_range'\n  what():  basic_string::substr: __pos (which is {last_colon_index_in_s + 2}) > this->size() (which is {6 + word.len()})". Observed pairs: (7,6) for '', (8,7) for ':', (9,8) for 'b:'/'A:'/'a'+':'/'::', (10,9) for ':a:'/':::', (11,10) for 'abc:', (12,11) for ':::::', (13,12) for X.'bcde:', (17,16) for 'a:b:c:d:e:', (18,17) for 'abcdefghij:', (60008,60007) for 60000x'a'+':'.

start == s.len() is NOT an error for substr -- it yields the empty string. That is why 'x', 'a:b', 'abc:d', 'abcdefg:h', $'\xba:b' produce an empty-but-present line 18 instead of aborting. Getting this off-by-one wrong flips the result between "" and a panic.
The function drops one byte too many: with no ':' in the word the result is word[1..], so ANY 1-byte word yields "". Faithful bug, not a transcription error.

The delimiter is the single byte 0x3A. Every other byte 0x01..0xFF was exhaustively verified non-delimiting from two different positions (763 dedicated probes), including '.', '/', ';', '|', '\\', '_', '-', '#', '$', space, TAB, 0x0D, 0x7F and all of 0x80..0xFF.
Slicing is byte-based and routinely produces invalid UTF-8 (bare continuation bytes 0xA9; 0x9F 0x98 0x80). The port must use Vec<u8>; &str indexing would panic where the C++ succeeds.
The prefix is exactly the 6 bytes "Test::" -- proven by the size term in the exception message being 6 + word.len() at m = 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 11 and 60001.

No other one of the 20 lines applies demodulize: classify('Foo::Bars') = 'Foo::Bar' and camelize/underscore/dasherize all preserve the '::', so the npos (colon-free) branch cannot be reached from this binary.

HARNESS CAVEAT: words containing 0x0A make stdout exceed 20 physical lines (word $'\n' -> 35 newlines, $'a\nb' -> 36), so `sed -n '18p'` is wrong for them. Match the expected trailing 4 lines instead. Also note bash `$(...)` strips trailing newlines, which is what made 0x0A look like an abort in the previous report.
Embedded NUL bytes cannot be passed through argv, so behavior on an interior 0x00 is unobservable.

uncertainties: truncate is only ever invoked with len = 5, so the internal decomposition `keep = len - omission.len()` (2 = 5 - 3) remains INFERRED. What is observed is the strictly weaker fact: size() <= 5 -> identity, size() >= 6 -> first 2 bytes + "...". Behavior for other len values -- especially len < 3, where the subtraction would underflow -- is unreachable from this harness. Likewise, whether truncate exposes omission/separator parameters with defaults (as ActiveSupport's does) is unobservable; I only proved that no separator or word-boundary snapping happens at len = 5 ('a bcdefgh' -> 0x61 0x20 '...', keeping a trailing space, rules out any rstrip/snap that WOULD be visible).

demodulize's npos branch (`if (pos == npos) return s;`) is UNREACHABLE through line 18: the argument is always "Test::" ++ word (6-byte prefix confirmed by the exception's size term at m = 0..60001), so pos >= 5 always. I additionally confirmed no other of the 20 lines routes through demodulize (classify/camelize/underscore/dasherize all preserve '::' verbatim), so this branch cannot be exercised by this binary at all. Returning `s` unchanged is the conventional implementation and is what hypothesis A asserts, but it is still not backed by an observation.

Byte 0x00 cannot be passed through argv, so neither function was tested with an embedded NUL. If the implementation internally touched a C string, a NUL would truncate early; std::string would not. Untestable from this harness.

Line 17's value is unobservable for exactly the inputs that make line 18 abort (the empty word, and any word whose last byte is 0x3A) -- e.g. truncate('abcdef:') can be predicted as 'ab...' but never observed, because the process emits no stdout at all in those runs.

Truncate was probed up to 100000 bytes and demodulize up to 60001 bytes. Behavior at sizes near ARG_MAX / allocation limits was not probed (arguments beyond ~128 KB start hitting the exec argument-size limit rather than the library).
